<a id="add-key-schedule-rows"></a>

### Add key schedule rows

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-16 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** fill an existing key table with new keys - one data row per Key Name.

Inserts data rows into a key table that already exists - one row per Key Name given, each name written and read back - so the drop-down on an element offers those keys. The other values of each key (the finish, the description) are filled after, the way any element's values are. **ITS ROWS ARE ITS KEYS.** A schedule of elements has no rows to insert - its rows are the model - so it is refused by name and left untouched. **A NAME ALREADY THERE IS LEFT ALONE**, and said: two keys of one name are two entries nobody can tell apart in a drop-down. The same name twice in one request is one key. **ALL OR NOTHING.** Revit is asked where a row may go before anything is inserted. A row that brings no key, or a name that does not read back, throws and the add-in rolls every key of the call back. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="create-schedule"></a>

### Create schedule

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-16 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** make a real schedule view of this category with these fields.

Creates a schedule view of one category, with the fields asked for, that lives in the project and can go on a sheet - a plain schedule, a sheet list, a view list or a key schedule, or (version 3) a material takeoff, a note block, a revision schedule, a keynote legend, or an area schedule of one area scheme. **A schedule and a count are different deliverables, and both are right answers to different sentences.** GROUP_AND_COUNT reads the model and puts numbers in the reply - which is what somebody wants when they ask *"how many of each size"*. This makes a view in the Project Browser that updates itself as the model changes and prints on a drawing. *"Make a schedule"* is the second one, and it was resolving to the first. **A field that the category does not have is reported, not skipped.** Ask for Size on a category with no Size parameter and a silently short schedule looks finished and is missing a column - and the person reading the drawing has no way to know a column was ever asked for. **VERSION 2 makes the other schedules too**, by `listKind`: a SHEET LIST - the drawing index, every sheet, placeholders included - or a VIEW LIST, both with their own fields and a sort; and a KEY SCHEDULE - a table of definitions elements point at, so one choice fills several fields - with its key parameter named and no rows yet. Sheets and views are not model elements, so the category route alone cannot make either.

<a id="export-schedule-to-csv"></a>

### Export schedule to CSV

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** write these schedules out as text files, and check the file is really there.

Writes schedules out as delimited text - the file that opens in Excel - and reports the paths that ACTUALLY EXIST ON DISK afterwards, the same read-back `EXPORT_SHEETS_TO_PDF` and `EXPORT_VIEWS_TO_DWG` use and for the same reason. IT EXISTS BECAUSE `FIND_SCHEDULES` ALREADY SAID IT DID. That fragment's own purpose names *"adding columns, exporting to CSV, placing on a sheet"* as the things it hands schedules to, and two of the three had never been built. `CREATE_SCHEDULE` carried a routing row reading *"nothing in the library exports anything yet"*, written when that was true and left standing after four export fragments landed. Measured before this batch, *"export this schedule to excel"* returned `FIND_SCHEDULES`, which finds the schedule and stops. **RISK IS PUBLISH, NOT MODIFY.** Nothing in the model changes. A file is written that gets emailed to a quantity surveyor, and one Ctrl+Z does not un-send it. That is a higher risk than editing the model, not a lower one. **IT WRITES WHAT THE SCHEDULE PRINTS, INCLUDING ITS FILTERS.** A schedule filtered to Level 2 exports Level 2. That is correct and it is the commonest misunderstanding in the whole cluster - somebody exporting "the duct schedule" and getting a third of the ducts has a filtered schedule, not a broken export. So the row count written is REPORTED, and `REPORT_SCHEDULE_DEFINITION` is named as the fragment that says why it is what it is. **THE DELIMITER IS A STATED INPUT.** A comma is the default and is wrong in every region whose decimal separator is a comma - the file opens as one column. Tab is the safe answer when that is in doubt, and it is the caller's call rather than a silent default that produces a plausible, useless file. **NO TRANSACTION, AND NONE IS NEEDED** - export is document I/O, not a model edit.

<a id="group-schedule-headers"></a>

### Group schedule headers

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** group neighbouring schedule column headings under one caption, or ungroup them.

Groups the headings of neighbouring schedule columns under one caption - "Size" over Width and Height - or ungroups a caption that is there. The first and last column are named by field name or printed heading, and every column between them in the schedule's order is in the group. Revit is asked whether the headings can be grouped before anything is written, and the table is read again afterwards to find the caption above the columns. A name answering to two columns touches neither; a hidden column is refused, because it has no heading on the sheet. The columns themselves - their data, headings and widths - are not changed. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="read-schedule-contents"></a>

### Read schedule contents

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-09 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** the rows this schedule actually prints, exactly as Revit prints them.

Reads the schedule's ROWS - the data it puts on the drawing - cell by cell, as the text Revit itself renders. It changes nothing. **IT READS THE PRINTED TEXT, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE POINT.** `ViewSchedule.GetCellText` hands back exactly what appears in the cell, which means every number arrives ALREADY FORMATTED IN THE PROJECT'S OWN UNITS - the duct is "450x250" because that is what the drawing says, not 1.4763779527 feet needing a conversion this fragment would have to guess at. That matters more than convenience. Reading the parameters instead would mean naming a units API to format them, and that call is the one that breaks at Revit 2021. Going through the rendered table sidesteps the whole problem and is simultaneously the more honest answer: **what the schedule says is what gets issued**, and any other reading is a reconstruction of it. IT EXISTS BECAUSE *"read me what is in the schedule"* AND *"the duct is missing from the schedule"* HAD NOWHERE TO GO. Measured before this batch, they resolved to `FIND_SCHEDULES` and `CREATE_SCHEDULE` - one finds the schedule and says nothing about its contents, the other makes a second schedule. Neither reads a row. **THE ROW COUNT IS THE ANSWER TO THE MISSING-ELEMENT QUESTION.** Somebody saying a duct is missing has a schedule whose filters or phase exclude it. This reports what IS there; `REPORT_SCHEDULE_DEFINITION` reports the rules that decided it. The pair answers the question and neither half does alone, which is why both name the other. **A LARGE SCHEDULE IS TRUNCATED AND SAYS SO.** A thousand-row takeoff read whole is not an answer anybody can read, and silently returning the first fifty would be a wrong answer wearing a right one's clothes. The cap is a stated input, the total is always reported, and the truncation is named.

<a id="remove-schedule-fields"></a>

### Remove schedule fields

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-09 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** take these columns out of the schedule, or hide them and keep the field.

Takes named columns out of a schedule - or HIDES them and keeps the field - and reports which of the two actually happened to each one. **IT EXISTS BECAUSE "REMOVE A COLUMN" WAS RESOLVING TO THE FRAGMENT THAT ADDS ONE.** Measured before this batch, *"remove a column from the schedule"* and *"take the level column out"* both returned `ADD_SCHEDULE_FIELDS`, which is not a near miss - it is the opposite operation, and it would have quietly put the column back that somebody asked to have taken away. **HIDING AND REMOVING ARE DIFFERENT JOBS AND BOTH ARE RIGHT ANSWERS.** | What you want | What to use | |---|---| | The column off the drawing, the data still available to sort and filter on | `hideOnly` - the field stays | | The field out of the schedule altogether | the default - it is gone | Somebody who sorts by Level but does not want a Level column wants the first one, and a fragment offering only the second breaks their schedule while doing exactly what they asked. **A FIELD USED BY A SORT OR A FILTER IS REFUSED, NOT SILENTLY CASCADED.** Revit will not let go of a field a rule still points at. Removing that rule too is often the right thing - but it is a SECOND change to the schedule that nobody asked for, and a schedule quietly losing its filter is exactly how a drawing goes out listing every level. So the rules are named, the removal is refused, and `removeDependentRules` is the caller saying yes to it. **THE FIELD ORDER IS RE-READ AFTERWARDS.** An absence of exception is not evidence that a field went - the standing lesson from the move and parameter paths. What is reported is what a second read found. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16), so clearing four columns off three schedules is one undo entry.

<a id="report-schedule-definition"></a>

### Report schedule definition

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-22 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** what this schedule is set up to do - its columns, its sorting, its filters.

Reads back how a schedule is CONFIGURED - the columns it carries, the order they sit in, what it sorts and groups by, what it filters out, and whether it totals. It changes nothing. IT EXISTS BECAUSE EVERY QUESTION ABOUT A SCHEDULE WAS BEING ANSWERED BY THE FRAGMENT THAT ADDS COLUMNS TO ONE. Measured against the library before this batch, *"what columns does this schedule have"*, *"show the schedule filter rules"* and *"what fields are in this schedule"* all resolved to `ADD_SCHEDULE_FIELDS` or `FIND_SCHEDULES`. The first is a **write** answering a question; the second finds the schedule and then has nothing to say about it. A question must not be answered by a fragment that modifies anything. **A HIDDEN COLUMN IS STILL A COLUMN, and that is the row worth reading.** Revit keeps a hidden field in the definition - it is in the schedule, it is simply not drawn. Somebody looking at the sheet and asking "where did the Level column go" is looking at a schedule that still HAS the Level column. Listing only what is visible would confirm their wrong guess, so hidden columns are listed and marked rather than omitted. **A FILTER'S NUMERIC VALUE IS REPORTED IN REVIT'S INTERNAL UNITS AND SAID TO BE.** A double filter value could be a length, an airflow, a pressure or an angle, and telling them apart needs the units API - which is the call that breaks at Revit 2021 and is forbidden here. So the number is handed back raw with the internal-units caveat attached rather than converted on a guess. A number converted by the wrong rule is worse than a number nobody converted: it looks finished. **A FILTER VALUE IS READ THROUGH THE GETTER THAT MATCHES ITS KIND.** Asking a string filter for its double value throws. Each filter is asked what kind of value it holds first, which is also the honest way to report a filter that holds no value at all - "has a value" and "is blank" are real filter types. **EVERY FILTER RULE IS LISTED, NUMBERED, IN ONE LINE (version 2).** `filterRules` holds each schedule's rules - "'DUCT HEATER SCHEDULE': 1. Type Mark equals 'MFD'; 2. Level equals 'FIRST FLOOR'" - each column by the heading it prints under (and its field name beside it when the heading was renamed), the match type in words, the value as Revit shows it. An element value - a Level rule holds the level, not its name - is shown by the element's NAME. A schedule with no rules says so. The numbers are the ones SET_SCHEDULE_FILTERS' `ruleNumber` counts with. One string, not a list, because a list is cut to three entries before anyone reads it - which is how four rules over two schedules came back as a count and nothing else.

<a id="set-schedule-appearance"></a>

### Set schedule appearance

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** how this schedule's columns read on the sheet - heading text, width, alignment, units, cell style.

Changes how a schedule's columns PRINT - the heading text, the column width, the alignment of the values, and whether the heading runs sideways. It changes no data and no element. IT EXISTS BECAUSE *"rename the column heading"*, *"make the schedule column wider"* and *"turn the schedule heading sideways"* all resolved to `ADD_SCHEDULE_FIELDS` or `CREATE_SCHEDULE` before this batch - a fragment that adds a column, and one that makes a second schedule. **THE HEADING AND THE FIELD NAME ARE DIFFERENT THINGS, AND ONLY ONE OF THEM PRINTS.** Renaming a heading to "Duct Size" leaves the field still called Size - so a later request to sort or filter *by Size* still works, and a request phrased *by Duct Size* has to find it by heading. That is why every fragment in this cluster matches on **either** name, and why this one reports both after the change. **WIDTH IS IN FEET BECAUSE IT IS A DISTANCE ON PAPER, AND IT ARRIVES IN mm.** `GridColumnWidth` is a Revit internal length like any other, so millimetres are divided by 304.8 as plain arithmetic at the edge - no units API, which is the call that breaks at 2021. A column width is one of the few numbers on a drawing that a modeller genuinely thinks about in millimetres. **A COLUMN'S BOLD IS THIS SCHEDULE'S OWN; A TEXT TYPE IS EVERYBODY'S.** Version 5 makes one column bold, italic, underlined, coloured, in another font or size - as an override on this schedule's column, the way Revit's Modify Schedule ribbon does it. It never edits the schedule's **text type**, which other schedules share - editing it would silently restyle drawings nobody asked about. **VERSION 5 SETS A COLUMN'S UNITS** - the Field Format of the Formatting tab, *"show the Length column in metres, 2 decimal places"*, or back to the project's units - and what a row prints when its elements disagree (Revit 2022 on). **VERSION 2 ADDS HIDING A COLUMN, WHICH IS NOT THE SAME AS REMOVING IT.** A field is often added to sort or filter by and is not meant to print. Hidden, it keeps doing that job off the drawing; removed, the sort goes with it and somebody rebuilds it later wondering what changed. It belongs here rather than in a fragment of its own: it is one more thing about how a column PRINTS, and a second fragment reaching into the same field would be two places to look. **VERSION 4 SWITCHES ON "CALCULATE TOTALS" for a column** - what each group footer and the grand total add up. Revit is asked first whether the column can be added up; one already totalling is left alone and said; a minimum or maximum it showed is reported as replaced; and each total says where it will print - or that it prints nowhere yet. A name that more than one column answers to, by field name or heading, now touches none of them, for every change here. **VERSION 5 GIVES THE REST OF THAT DROP-DOWN** - minimum, maximum, minimum and maximum, or no calculation - asked of Revit first in the same way (`CanDisplayMinMax` for a minimum or maximum). ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="set-schedule-field-order"></a>

### Set schedule field order

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** put a schedule's columns in a new order - move a column up, down, before or after another.

Puts a schedule's columns in a new order - the Fields tab's Move Up and Move Down, in one call. Name the columns in the order wanted ("Mark, Size, Length") and they go first, in that order, with every other column keeping its own order after them; or move one column - to a place, to the front or the end, or before or after another column. **A PLACE IS A PLACE IN THE FIELDS TAB'S LIST, AND HIDDEN FIELDS COUNT.** That list shows hidden fields and so does the order Revit keeps, so "move Length to 2" makes Length the second field there. On the printed schedule the column can sit further left when a hidden field comes before it, and the order read back marks the hidden ones. **A COLUMN IS FOUND BY ITS FIELD NAME OR ITS PRINTED HEADING, AND A NAME THAT ANSWERS TO TWO COLUMNS MOVES NOTHING.** Every name is resolved before anything is written; a schedule with one unknown, ambiguous or repeated name is left exactly as it was and named, and the other schedules still go on. **THE ORDER REPORTED IS READ BACK, NOT ECHOED.** Revit is always handed the whole order, every field once, and the order it then holds is what comes back. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

**How to use it**

<a id="set-schedule-filters"></a>

### Set schedule filters

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-22 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** filter this schedule down to the rows that match, without touching any element.

Sets the filter rules on a schedule - which rows it shows - and changes NOTHING about any element in the model. **IT EXISTS BECAUSE THE SENTENCE IT ANSWERS WAS RESOLVING TO A FRAGMENT THAT EDITS ELEMENTS.** Measured before this batch, *"filter the schedule to level 2 only"* returned `SET_ELEMENT_LEVEL`. That is not a near miss and it is not a wasted call: the request is to hide rows in a table, and the fragment it reached MOVES DUCTS TO ANOTHER LEVEL. This is the exact shape the whole project exists around - an answer that looks like it worked and has changed the wrong thing. **"BY LEVEL" MEANS TWO DIFFERENT JOBS AND BOTH GET SAID THE SAME WAY.** Filtering decides WHICH rows appear; sorting decides what ORDER they come in. *"Do it by level"* is either. `SET_SCHEDULE_SORT_GROUP` carries this same row, because which of the two a search returns is not something either fragment chooses. **THE FIELD MUST BE A COLUMN BEFORE IT CAN BE FILTERED ON, AND REVIT DECIDES WHICH COLUMNS ARE FILTERABLE.** `CanFilterByValue` is its own answer and is asked before anything is written. A schedule cannot filter on a field it does not carry - which is why *"filter to level 2"* on a schedule with no Level column is refused with that reason rather than with an exception. **THE MATCH TYPE IS A STATED INPUT, NOT GUESSED FROM THE VALUE.** "Equals", "contains" and "begins with" produce different drawings from the same word, and inferring one from the shape of the text is how a schedule silently includes Level 20 when somebody asked for Level 2. **LEFT TO ITSELF IT REPLACES THE FILTERS, NOT ADDS TO THEM**, and what was there is reported before it goes. A schedule that accumulates filters shows fewer and fewer rows, and each addition looks correct on its own. Adding happens only when asked for (version 2). **CHANGING ONE KEEPS THE OTHERS (version 2).** A change alters one rule's value or match type and leaves the rest as they were; a remove takes one out. Two rules on one column are refused until `ruleNumber` says which - picking the first is a guess. Nothing is written until the whole new set is known, and a refusal from Revit puts the old set back. **A NEW VALUE IS WRITTEN AS TEXT, AND THAT IS A DELIBERATE LIMIT.** A numeric filter value would have to be handed to Revit in internal units, and knowing which unit a given parameter uses needs the units API - the call that breaks at Revit 2021 and is forbidden here. Text rules cover the sentences that were measured; a number rule would work on one release and silently mis-scale on another, which is worse than not offering it. A changed rule that points at an element - a Level rule - takes another element's NAME instead, looked up among elements of the same kind. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

| | |
|---|---|
| **Kind** | Changes the model (`MODIFY`) |
| **Reached by** | asking in a Claude chat |
| **Works on** | what is selected in Revit: elements |
| **You say** | **filter field name** - text; optional, left out means *none*<br>**filter value** - text; optional, left out means *keep*<br>**match type** - text; optional, left out means *keep*<br>**filter action** - text; optional, left out means *replace*<br>**rule number** - a whole number - digits only - 250, not 250mm; optional, left out means *0*<br>**filter rules** - text; optional, left out means *none* |
| **You get** | filtered, applied rules, rules after |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2020 |
| **Capability** | `SET_SCHEDULE_FILTERS` |

<a id="set-schedule-options"></a>

### Set schedule options

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** the schedule's own settings - title, headers, grid lines, text types, striped rows, row height, linked files, filter by sheet, embedded schedule.

Sets a schedule's own settings - not a column's: Show Title, Show Headers and Grid lines on sheets; which text type its Title, Header and Body text use; Striped rows, striped rows on sheets and the stripe colour; the row height (Revit 2024 and later); Include elements in links; Filter by sheet (Revit 2023 and later); and an embedded schedule, added or removed. Only what is named is changed, each is read back, and one setting the schedule cannot take is named while the others are still set. **A TEXT TYPE IS CHOSEN, NOT EDITED.** Bold, font and size belong to a text type other schedules share; this changes which type THIS schedule uses, so "make the schedule text bold" is served by choosing a bold text type and no other drawing changes. **FREEZE HEADERS IS NOT HERE.** It is a switch of the Revit session, not a setting saved in the model. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="set-schedule-sort-group"></a>

### Set schedule sort group

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** sort and group this schedule by these fields, with headers and totals.

Sets what a schedule sorts and groups by - in order - and whether each level gets a header, a footer and a blank line, plus the grand total at the bottom. IT EXISTS BECAUSE *"sort the schedule by level"* RESOLVED TO `LIST_LEVELS`. Measured before this batch: a question about the levels in the project, returned for a sentence about the order of rows in a schedule. Nothing in the library could sort anything. **SORTING AND GROUPING ARE ONE CONTROL IN REVIT, AND THAT SURPRISES PEOPLE.** There is no separate "group by". A field with `showHeader` on IS a group - the header is the band carrying the level name across the sheet. So *"group the schedule by system type"* and *"sort it by system type"* are the same call with one flag different, and the flag is the entire difference between a grouped schedule and a long flat list. **"COLLAPSE THE ROWS" IS `itemized`, NOT A SORT, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT CHANGES THE ROW COUNT.** Turning itemising off makes identical elements share one row - which is what somebody means by *"just show me one line per size"*. It is set here because it is on the same Revit tab and is meaningless without the sorting beneath it. **A FIELD THE SCHEDULE CANNOT SORT BY IS ASKED ABOUT BEFORE IT IS TRIED.** `CanSortByField` is Revit's own answer, and it covers the cases that are otherwise exceptions half way through a batch that has already changed the first two fields. **THE SORT IS REPLACED, NOT APPENDED TO.** Asking for "sort by level" on a schedule already sorted by mark means sorted by level - not sorted by mark then level. Appending is how a schedule ends up with four sort levels nobody chose, and the existing rules are reported before they go. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).
